# SYNTHETIC: How undergraduates experience structured reading logs, an interview study

> SYNTHETIC SOURCE. This is a fictional study written for an evaluation exercise. It does not describe real research, real participants, or real authors, and it must not be cited as evidence outside this workspace.

Keiko Tanaka-Reyes (2024). Synthetic Qualitative Studies in Higher Education (fictional), 2(3).

## Abstract

This synthetic qualitative study interviewed 24 undergraduates who had used structured reading logs in a research methods course, using reflexive thematic analysis.

## Methods

Semi-structured interviews lasted 40 to 60 minutes. Participants came from three course sections at one institution. Transcripts were coded inductively by the author and checked by a second reader.

## Findings

Students described the log prompts as a checklist that slowed them down before they trusted a source. Several students said the log made them notice when they did not know who had written a page. Students whose logs were ungraded described the log as busywork and reported filling it in after writing the paper.

## Limitations

The sample came from a single institution and was self-selected. Interview accounts describe perceived change and do not measure source evaluation performance.

# SYNTHETIC: Reading logs paired with one-shot library instruction and lateral reading behavior

> SYNTHETIC SOURCE. This is a fictional study written for an evaluation exercise. It does not describe real research, real participants, or real authors, and it must not be cited as evidence outside this workspace.

Rania Haddad, Tomas Moreno (2022). Synthetic Review of Academic Librarianship (fictional), 9(1).

## Abstract

This synthetic quasi-experimental study compared 148 undergraduates who completed a reading log after one-shot library instruction with peers who received instruction alone. Screen-recorded tasks showed more lateral reading in the log group.

## Methods

Two intact sections of an introductory research course served as the log group and two as the comparison group. All students received the same 50-minute library session. Lateral reading, defined as leaving a source to check it elsewhere, was coded from screen recordings of a timed web evaluation task at pre-test and post-test.

## Results

In the log group, the share of students who read laterally rose from 18% at pre-test to 37% at post-test. In the comparison group, the share rose from 16% to 21% over the same period.

## Limitations

Sections were not randomized, and the log group instructor had more teaching experience. The study did not report a rubric-based quality score, so behavior change cannot be linked to better judgments.

# SYNTHETIC: Reading logs without instructor feedback, a randomized trial with delayed follow-up

> SYNTHETIC SOURCE. This is a fictional study written for an evaluation exercise. It does not describe real research, real participants, or real authors, and it must not be cited as evidence outside this workspace.

Declan Brennan, Liesbeth Achterberg (2021). Synthetic Journal of College Learning (fictional), 11(4).

## Abstract

This synthetic randomized trial assigned 96 undergraduates to complete a structured reading log or a free-form reading journal, with no instructor feedback in either arm. Source evaluation was measured immediately and six weeks later.

## Methods

Students in a general education seminar were individually randomized. The log used the same four prompts as prior log designs, but logs were collected only for completion credit. The outcome was a 24-point source evaluation rubric scored by raters blinded to condition.

## Results

At the immediate post-test, the log group scored 0.3 points higher than the journal group on the 24-point rubric (d = 0.08), a difference that was not statistically significant. At the six-week follow-up, the groups did not differ.

## Limitations

The trial was powered to detect only moderate effects. Completion-only credit may have encouraged rapid, low-effort log entries.

# SYNTHETIC: Structured reading logs and source evaluation in first-year composition, a cluster randomized trial

> SYNTHETIC SOURCE. This is a fictional study written for an evaluation exercise. It does not describe real research, real participants, or real authors, and it must not be cited as evidence outside this workspace.

Amara Okafor, Signe Lindqvist (2023). Synthetic Journal of Information Literacy (fictional), 4(2).

## Abstract

This synthetic cluster randomized trial assigned 12 first-year composition sections to a structured reading log or to standard annotation. Across 312 students, the log condition scored 2.1 points higher on a 24-point source evaluation rubric at post-test (d = 0.41).

## Methods

Twelve sections were randomized at the section level, six to each condition. The structured reading log asked students to record, for every source, the author's credentials, the publisher, the evidence offered, and one corroborating outside source. Instructors returned written feedback on logs every two weeks. The outcome was a 24-point source evaluation rubric applied by two blinded raters to an annotated bibliography (inter-rater ICC = 0.86).

## Results

At post-test, students in the reading log sections scored 2.1 points higher on the 24-point rubric than students in annotation sections (d = 0.41, 95% CI 0.18 to 0.64). The largest gain appeared on the rubric item for checking claims against an outside source.

## Limitations

Only 12 clusters were randomized, so the confidence interval is wide. Instructors were not blinded, and the study measured a single course term without a delayed post-test.

# Protocol: Structured reading logs and undergraduate source evaluation

> SYNTHETIC REVIEW. Every study in this workspace is a fictional example created for an evaluation exercise. No real literature was searched, and no finding here should be cited as evidence about real students.

## Research question (2026-10-08)

Among undergraduate students, do structured reading logs, compared with unstructured note-taking, annotation, or no log, improve source evaluation performance or behavior?

- **Population**: undergraduate students in any discipline or course.
- **Intervention**: a structured reading log, meaning a recurring template with fixed prompts about a source (for example author, publisher, evidence, corroboration) completed while reading.
- **Comparison**: annotation, free-form journals or notes, instruction without a log, or no intervention.
- **Outcomes**: source evaluation quality (rubric or test scores), source evaluation behavior (for example lateral reading), or student-reported experience of evaluating sources.

## Inclusion criteria

1. Participants are undergraduates (or results are reported separately for undergraduates).
2. The intervention includes a structured reading log as defined above.
3. At least one outcome concerns source evaluation quality, behavior, or experience.
4. Empirical design: randomized, quasi-experimental, or qualitative primary study.
5. English language; any publication year.
6. Marked as a synthetic example study (task constraint for this evaluation workspace).

## Exclusion criteria

1. Secondary school, graduate, or professional populations only.
2. Reading logs used only for reading volume or comprehension, with no source evaluation outcome.
3. Opinion pieces, teaching tips without data, or reviews.

## Approval checkpoint

The skill asks for user approval of criteria at the end of Scope. This run is in evaluation capture mode and non-interactive, so the criteria above were recorded without a pause. Approval status: **not obtained; recorded for evaluator review**.

### Literature Review: Structured reading logs and undergraduate source evaluation

> SYNTHETIC REVIEW. All four included studies are fictional examples created for an evaluation exercise and are labeled SYNTHETIC in their titles. They describe no real research, and nothing below should be read as evidence about real students.

**Research question**: Among undergraduate students, do structured reading logs, compared with unstructured note-taking, annotation, or no log, improve source evaluation performance or behavior?

**Inclusion criteria**: Undergraduate population; a structured reading log with fixed prompts about each source; an outcome on source evaluation quality, behavior, or experience; randomized, quasi-experimental, or qualitative primary design; English; any year; synthetic example studies only.

**Searches executed**:
- No OpenAlex, arXiv, or Europe PMC query was executed. The task restricts the corpus to synthetic example studies, so the pool was built directly from synthetic records (see `protocol.md`).

## Thematic synthesis

### Effects on source evaluation quality depend on feedback

In a cluster randomized trial across 12 first-year composition sections and 312 students, structured reading logs with biweekly instructor feedback raised scores on a 24-point source evaluation rubric by 2.1 points (d = 0.41) (Okafor et al., 2023). The largest gain appeared on the rubric item for checking claims against an outside source (Okafor et al., 2023). Because only 12 clusters were randomized and there was no delayed post-test, the precision and durability of this effect remain uncertain (Okafor et al., 2023). This trial is the strongest design in the set, with blinded raters, though its cluster count is small.

In a randomized trial of 96 undergraduates where logs earned completion credit only and received no instructor feedback, the log group scored just 0.3 points higher on the same 24-point rubric (d = 0.08), and the groups did not differ at a six-week follow-up (Brennan et al., 2021). The authors note that completion-only credit may have encouraged rapid, low-effort log entries (Brennan et al., 2021). Individual randomization and a delayed measure make this a well-controlled null result, but the trial was small and powered only for moderate effects.

Read together, the two trials point to feedback as a plausible moderator. The log template was similar across them, while the presence of instructor response differed. With only two trials, this remains a hypothesis and not an established finding.

### Effects on evaluation behavior

A quasi-experimental study of 148 undergraduates found that the share of students who read laterally rose from 18% to 37% when a reading log followed one-shot library instruction, compared with a rise from 16% to 21% after instruction alone (Haddad et al., 2022). Sections were not randomized and no rubric-based quality score was reported, so the study shows a behavioral shift without showing better judgments (Haddad et al., 2022). Its contribution is behavioral evidence from screen recordings, and its quality is moderate given the instructor confound.

### How students experience reading logs

Interviews with 24 undergraduates describe log prompts as a checklist that slowed students down before they trusted a source (Tanaka-Reyes, 2024). Students whose logs were ungraded described the log as busywork and reported completing it after writing the paper (Tanaka-Reyes, 2024). This single-site, self-selected qualitative study offers a mechanism (slowing down and prompting corroboration) and an implementation risk (retroactive completion), but it does not measure performance.

### Overall assessment

The synthetic evidence is mixed and thin. A log with regular instructor feedback was associated with a modest rubric gain and more corroboration, while a log collected for completion only showed no measurable benefit. Behavioral and interview evidence is consistent with a slowing-down mechanism that weakens when students treat the log as busywork. Confidence in any overall effect is low.

## Research gaps

1. No included study manipulated feedback directly within a single trial, so the feedback-as-moderator account rests on comparison across studies with different populations and courses.
2. Only one study measured a delayed outcome, and it found no effect. Durability after a log-supported course is unknown.
3. No study linked observed lateral reading to rubric-scored judgment quality in the same students.
4. All studies came from single institutions, and none reported results by prior information literacy instruction, discipline, or first-generation status.
